newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian markets soar as budget brightens outlook.
newsitem.headline: Italian markets soar as budget brightens outlook.

text.p: Italian financial markets on Friday soared on a wave of euphoria that tougher than expected 1997 budget-cutting measures will thrust the nation into the front line for membership of the single European currency.

Analysts said bonds, the lira and shares responded positively to the centre-left government's determination to adhere to strick financial discipline. But they hoped the Bank of Italy would act soon to cut interest rates to offset any dampening effect the harsh 1997 financial package would have on economic growth.

In early trading, Italian domestic bonds surged to touch historic highs, the lira continued firm after touching its highest level against the German mark since early August 1994 in late Thursday trading, while shares were swept higher.

The Italian cabinet was meeting on Friday to approve the budget which will cut some 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off Italy's large deficit, well in excess of the 32.4 trillion the government had originally planned to cut in its three-year economic plan.

The budget is to include a special "Euro-tax" which is seen as raising 12.5 trillion lire. After cabinet approval on Friday the whole 1997 financial package will be submitted to parliament which must pass it into law by the end of December.

"The optimism is justified, the budget cuts are bigger than expected, while the big surprise is that it appears to have the support of the Communists," said Francesco Giordano senior economist at Italy's San Paolo Bank.

Italy's centre-left government led by prime minister Romano Rrodi and appointed in May, relies on the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party for its majority in the lower house of parliament.
The Communists are opposed to cuts in health and pension spending, but their leader Fausto Bertinotti said on Thursday that budget talks with the government had made progress.

In the bond market, BTP Italian government bonds futures on London's LIFFE market swept away resistance levels and quickly moved into uncharted territory, as the December BTP contract hit a record high of 122.50 and at 1100 GMT traded up 1.39 percentage points at 121.82.
Dealers and analysts said that the market was consolidating after some dramatic gains, but there was still further room for increases and a narrowing of spreads against German bunds.
The Italian currency held around 1,000 lire to the mark after hitting a new high of 994.40 lire late Thursday, the highest level seen since early August 1994
Shares on the Milan bourse were also driven higher with the all-share Mibtel index up 2.34 percent at 10,080 and the Mib30 index of Italy's 30 biggest companies up 2.65 percent.

The financial package is aimed at cutting Italy's deficit to gross domestic product ratio to three percent in 1997, a key target set out in the Maastricht Treaty for European Union members to join a single European currency in 1999.

Analyst said that the government was now talking about meeting the 3 percent target by 1997 for the first time. Orignally under the three year plan it was to be 1998. They said this aim was tough but not impossible to reach.
But analysts pointed out that interest rates would need to be cut to offset the likely fall in Italian economic growth that could result from the tough deficit-cutting budget.

San Paolo's Giordano is looking for two interest cuts by the end of the year. One of 0.75 percentage points in October and and further one of 0.5 points by the end of the year to bring Italy's discount rate down to 7.0 percent.
He sees a slowdown in growth from the budget, but a long period of lower growth rather than a recession.

Most other analysts see an interest rate cut by the end of the year despite a statement from the Bank of Italy that it will keep monetary policy tight to push average inflation below three percent. Official Italian inflation in August was 3.4 percent. ($1=1,521 lire)
